pull.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pull.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

I don't think it's a good idea to change the node's behaviour in a way that doesn't allow users/miners to revert to the previous default in case the change turns out to be undesirable or harmful for some or many users.

Is there any reason why this change shouldn't be phased in via setting `DEFAULT_MEMPOOL_EXPIRY_HOURS` to a large value, such as 35040 (4 years), instead?

Concept ACK

Node operators should assume that at any point in time, and for any duration of time, their mempool can consume up to `-maxmempool` of resources. Of course, we should make the mempool maximally useful within that constraint, and transactions that should (from the node's perspective) get mined, but don't, can affect its ability to hold transactions that actually will/can get mined.

The main downside from this removal is that in a non-adversarial case (an adversary can just rebroadcast every 2 weeks), transactions can remain in the mempool forever with a high enough fee rate, e.g. in case of diverging policy or consensus rules, and this reduces a node's effective mempool capacity. While that is not ideal, I also don't think we need to have startup options that make it easier to run a node that is out of sync with the policy and consensus rules that the network actually operates on.

I think the other historically mentioned reasons don't hold up anymore either:
- it's nice to be able to replace a large, low fee rate transaction without having to pay the RBF "tax", but RBF mitigates free relay for a reason, I don't think we need a carve-out, even a conservatively rate-limited one
- pinning attacks also seem largely irrelevant, given the 2 week delay and the fact that we have TRUC now

> Is there any reason why this change shouldn't be phased in via setting

I think it's nice that we can clean up the code right away. If people can come up with good reasons to use this setting, it might make sense to keep it, or deprecate rather than remove. But if we can't, then I think it's sensible to remove it?

Two things look unfinished: the memory estimate still counts three indexes, and `wallet_resendwallettransactions.py` no longer checks that a parent is resubmitted before its child.

tumutech's inline question on the first is still open. `getmempoolinfo` reports `usage` 1192 for one transaction on both 649bc0a (base) and 1556184 (head), since `DynamicMemoryUsage()` still counts 9 pointers per entry. The old resend test expired a parent and child and needed both resubmitted, which works only in insertion order. With that order reversed, base's test fails (`resubmit 1`) and head's passes.

Could this PR use 6 pointers, as tumutech suggests, or drop the "fits slightly more transactions" sentence? For the test, restarting with `-persistmempool=0` and checking that both transactions are back would make the order matter again, since the wallet resubmits them on load.

The rest matches the release note. I measured it with a functional-test script on regtest with mocktime, and the touched functional tests and the unit suite pass on head on macOS (the USDT test skipped). Head keeps transactions past 336 h, loads older `mempool.dat` entries with their entry time, and warns that `-mempoolexpiry` has no effect. One change may deserve a line in the note: `abandontransaction` on a wallet transaction older than two weeks now fails with "Transaction not eligible for abandonment". On base it worked after expiry, until the wallet's next resubmission, within 36 h, put it back. I can share the script as a gist.

I've spent some time going through the discussion in[ #33510](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33510) and the history of mempool expiry. I agree that removing transactions simply because they've been in the mempool for 14 days isn't ideal, especially when an old parent could become attractive through a new high-fee child.

My main concern with removing expiry entirely is the possibility of retaining high-feerate transactions that miners won't include, for example when an outdated node accepts transactions that violate newer policies adopted by miners, such as[ #32521](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32521). `TrimToSize()` wouldn't necessarily help here, since those transactions are still highly ranked locally. Under memory pressure, they could displace lower-feerate transactions that miners would actually include, potentially causing more `SIZELIMIT` removals and raising the minimum mempool feerate.

I agree with **stickies-v** that this mostly concerns outdated nodes, and expiry isn't particularly effective against an attacker who keeps rebroadcasting. However, it does provide eventual recovery from a one-time attack or persistent policy disagreement when the transactions are no longer being submitted.

The data shared by **0xB10C** shows that expiry removes transactions that can later be mined, but I'm not sure it tells us enough about the tradeoff. How often does expiry remove economically attractive transactions or CPFP packages, compared with how often it actually frees capacity occupied by transactions miners won't include? And would removing it lead to more size-based evictions or a higher minimum mempool feerates under pressure?

Looking at the hybrid approach suggested by **Ismaelsadeeq**, i.e combining transaction age with missed mining opportunities, possibly only under memory pressure. I'm leaning toward exploring this longer term, but it has its own problems. Local template inclusion doesn't establish that miners received or rejected a transaction, and counting missed opportunities could penalize censored transactions. There are also the costs of template construction and the question of what happens to previous observations when a parent receives a new high-fee child.

There's also the interaction with fee estimation following[ #34075](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34075). Persistently unmined, high-feerate transactions could affect the mempool-based estimator despite its health checks. But I think that such transactions for estimation don't require removing them from the mempool. I think this is worth investigating separately, rather than using fee estimation as a reason to retain expiry.

Given this, I'm leaning toward deprecating `-mempoolexpiry` rather than removing its functionality immediately, with age expiry disabled by default but still available explicitly during the deprecation period. This would preserve a recovery option for operators while giving us a chance to understand the consequences of the changed default.

Finally, Is there already evidence that the protection expiry provides against persistent policy disagreement is negligible enough to justify removing the mechanism entirely, rather than just changing the default?

I'd appreciate corrections in case I missed something.

events.body:
Thanks for review @ajtowns @stickies-v @maflcko @tumutech @fametrano @musaHaruna 

I addressed most feedback and concerns in the latest push or with reply below.

> My main concern with removing expiry entirely is the possibility of retaining high-feerate transactions that miners won't include ... Under memory pressure, they could displace lower-feerate transactions that miners would actually include, potentially causing more SIZELIMIT removals and raising the minimum mempool feerate.

The best thing to do in this case is to update the node, because expiry doesn't help here either. The transactions can just be rebroadcast again, and as you mentioned, this cycle can go on forever, so I don't think this is a valid reason to keep expiry.

> How often does expiry remove economically attractive transactions or CPFP packages, compared with how often it actually frees capacity occupied by transactions miners won't include? And would removing it lead to more size-based evictions or a higher minimum mempool feerates under pressure?

I think the fact that it is possible, and that we see such transactions mined, should suffice. We assume miners act rationally and follow incentive compatibility for inclusion, so whatever they mine is economically incentive compatible at that moment in time.

> Looking at the hybrid approach suggested by Ismaelsadeeq ... counting missed opportunities could penalize censored transactions ...

There is a legitimate concern raised by @mzumsande, and offline by a few other people, that this approach also aids censorship, so I won't be comfortable shipping it.

> There's also the interaction with fee estimation following #34075 ...

I thought about this, and that's why the default never uses the mempool to raise the fee rate estimate, so it's not going to be a problem at all. It may only affect users who explicitly request the mempool estimator alone, and I assume those are advanced users who know what they're getting into and should have a sentinel max, e.g. an LND budget sweeper.

> Given this, I'm leaning toward deprecating -mempoolexpiry rather than removing its functionality immediately, with age expiry disabled by default but still available explicitly during the deprecation period.

I feel strongly about this. I think the reasons mentioned above by you and @ajtowns are thin. We should not incentivize free relay, the expiry use case is a bit speculative, and @0xB10C's data already showed that most of the expired txs eventually get mined. In the adversarial scenario expiry won't help either, since the attacker can just keep cycling it. The fee rate estimator is not affected. So it would be more ideal to just clean this code up and remove this feature, it is unnecessary.

Also, if we decide to remove wallet rebroadcast and only rebroadcast what's not in the mempool, we would still have a privacy leak if users expire, because we'd expire our own txs and then rebroadcast them again. The same thing happens on reload: loading mempool.dat drops entries older than the expiry, so after a restart the node treats its own aged txs as missing and rebroadcasts them.

events.message:
mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry

Evicting transactions purely by age (-mempoolexpiry, default two weeks)
is incentive-incompatible: it can drop still-mineable transactions, such
as a low-feerate parent waiting on a fee-bumping child. Remove it;
-mempoolexpiry is kept as a no-op that warns when set.

mempool: remove now-unused entry_time index and includes

Expire() was the only reader of the entry_time index. Keeping it would
cost an ordered-tree node per entry and an O(log n) update on every
mempool insert/erase to maintain an ordering nothing uses, so drop the
index along with its tag, comparator, and the boost headers only it
needed. identity.hpp is then unused tree-wide, so also drop it from
EXPECTED_BOOST_INCLUDES, and lower the DynamicMemoryUsage() per-entry
estimate from three indexes to two so -maxmempool accounting stays
accurate.

Also move util/time.h into txmempool.h (it uses GetTime/chrono) instead
of relying on mempool_options.h, and drop the unused <chrono> and
<memory> from mempool_args.cpp.
